analysis.one_liner: Bans exporting pesticides banned in the U.S. and requires disclosure of pesticides on imported food.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the 105th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped a practice known as the 'circle of poison': American companies exporting pesticides that are banned or restricted in the United States to other countries, whose residue can then return on imported food. It would have required that exported pesticides be labeled in the buying country's language, that the buying country consent to the shipment, and that U.S. pesticide manufacturers report what they ship abroad. It also would have required food importers to disclose which pesticides were used on their products and tightened the rules linking a pesticide's U.S. cancellation to revoking its legal residue limits on food.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers of imported fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, and eggs, who would face tighter monitoring and disclosure of pesticide residues on those foods. Farmworkers and residents in developing countries, who would no longer receive pesticides the EPA has deemed too dangerous for U.S. use. The EPA and FDA, which would gain export data and import disclosures that make residue monitoring more targeted.

how_it_helps.text: Bars export of any pesticide whose active ingredient has had its U.S. registrations canceled, its food tolerances revoked, or been ruled ineligible for reregistration, closing the 'circle of poison' by which products deemed too dangerous for American farms are shipped abroad.

Requires exported pesticide labels to be written in an official language of the country of use and to carry the same health and safety information required on U.S. labels, and requires notice and consent from the destination country before shipment of the most hazardous pesticides.

Lets any person sue in federal court to impose civil penalties on exporters who violate the export rules, with half of any penalty going to the person who brought the suit, supplementing government enforcement.

Requires importers of raw agricultural commodities, meat, poultry, and eggs to file documents identifying each pesticide used in producing them, and to submit residue analyses if unreported pesticides are detected, giving the FDA better information for monitoring imported food.

Automatically revokes or suspends the legal residue limits (tolerances) on food when a pesticide's U.S. registration is canceled or suspended for health reasons, so a banned pesticide cannot keep a legal pathway onto food.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, which would lose the ability to sell domestically banned or canceled products overseas and would bear new reporting, labeling, and notification costs. Food importers, which would bear new documentation and testing duties. Foreign buyers, who would lose access to cheap U.S. pesticides no longer registered here, though the bill allows temporary waivers for disease outbreaks and famine emergencies.

drawbacks.text: Poorer countries could lose access to inexpensive U.S. pesticides for agricultural pest control, and the bill only waives its restrictions for communicable disease and famine emergencies, not for ordinary crop losses.

The compliance burden is substantial: manufacturers must report exports and notify destination countries, and importers must document every pesticide used abroad, which could raise food import costs and add to FDA and EPA administrative workloads.

The citizen-lawsuit provision allows private plaintiffs to collect half of any civil penalty imposed on an exporter, which critics of such provisions generally argue invites litigation; the bill does cap sanctions for bad-faith suits at $5,000.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections for consumers and for people in exporting-destination countries are substantial and directly targeted at a documented mechanism of harm, and it contains real accommodations: temporary waivers for disease and famine emergencies, an experimental-use pathway with foreign consent, and relief for residues attributable to long-term environmental persistence. The main costs fall on manufacturers and importers as compliance burdens and lost export markets, with some risk of higher food prices; the citizen-suit mechanism is the most contestable design choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of a Congress that was about to expire, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and nothing further ever happened to it.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on October 21, 1998, less than three weeks before the 105th Congress's end-of-session period.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which held no hearing, took no vote, and never reported it out before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and food importers are better off, because the export bans, labeling rules, consent requirements, and import disclosure obligations never took effect and the existing practice of exporting pesticides banned for U.S. use continued.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 21, 1998 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no one joined the sponsor, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from exporting pesticides whose U.S. registrations were canceled or whose food tolerances were revoked, ending a profitable foreign market for products deemed too dangerous for domestic use. It also imposed new reporting, labeling, and notification duties on export shipments.

Importers would have had to document every pesticide used on their products at entry and submit residue analyses when unreported pesticides were found. Their interest in avoiding that scrutiny runs against the consumer interest in knowing what residues are on imported food.
Consumers would get stronger residue monitoring and disclosure on imported food and, over time, fewer banned-pesticide residues returning on food grown abroad with U.S.-banned chemicals.
